title: PixelBench: Can LLMs Understand andGenerate Images Pixel by Pixel?

paper.title: PixelBench: Can LLMs Understand and Generate Images Pixel by Pixel?
paper.abstract: Abstract Large language models (LLMs) can generate visual assets through text-based formats such as SVG and CAD, but these symbolic representations describe images using high-level primitives rather than explicit raster values. We ask whether LLMs can instead generate pixel images directly through their existing vocabulary, without a learned image tokenizer or decoder. We introduce PixelBench, a benchmark for text-to-pixel (T2P) and image-to-pixel (I2P) generation across multiple resolutions, together with a complementary pixel-understanding evaluation. Models generate an RGB color palette followed by a grid of indices specifying the palette color of each output pixel. In T2P, the strongest models produce recognizable images directly from text. In I2P, the strongest models outperform palette-matched downsampling and specialized pixelization algorithms at low resolutions. Pixel-understanding performance correlates strongly with generation performance. A resolution-scaling study shows that pixel-generation performance often improves initially before declining at high resolutions. Finally, we introduce Pixel Reconstruction Tuning (PRT), which augments visual instruction tuning with caption-palette-grid trajectories. We post-train Molmo2-4B from its pretraining checkpoint by mixing general instruction data with our curated PRT data, improving performance across 16 visual-centric benchmarks, indicating that explicit pixel reconstruction can provide useful auxiliary supervision.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Large language models (LLMs) were originally developed to predict the next token in natural-language sequences. The same autoregressive training paradigm has since produced strong code-generation capabilities. Some generated code, including SVG code and CAD programs, can be rendered into images, providing an interface for probing how LLMs express visual information ( Sharma et al., 2024 ; Qiu et al., 2025 ; Chen et al., 2026b ; Rodriguez et al., 2025 ; Xing et al., 2025 ; Khan et al., 2024 ) . However, these formats describe images using semantically meaningful, high-level primitives and are therefore one step away from actual visual appearance: a renderer expands each primitive into many pixels. By contrast, RGB rasters provide a more direct and ubiquitous representation of digital images, with each spatial location in a two-dimensional grid storing a color value. Most modern image generators map learned visual tokens or latent representations to pixels through dedicated decoders ( Chameleon Team, 2024 ; Wang et al., 2026 ) . Prior work has also trained specialized autoregressive image models to generate images directly in raster space ( van den Oord et al., 2016a ; van den Oord et al., 2016b ; Parmar et al., 2018 ; Chen et al., 2020 ) . These studies demonstrate the feasibility of direct pixel generation, but rely on models specifically designed and trained for image modeling. To better investigate pixel-based visual understanding and generation, we ask the following question: Can LLMs directly generate and understand visual content pixel by pixel? To address this research question, we introduce PixelBench , a benchmark for evaluating LLMs on direct pixel generation and understanding. PixelBench uses a palette-indexed raster representation: the model first defines a palette of up to eight RGB colors and then generates a grid of palette indices, with each grid position specifying the color of one pixel. This interface needs no learned tokenizer, image decoder, or architectural change. PixelBench evaluates three tasks: text-to-pixel generation (T2P), where a model generates a recognizable pixel image from an object label, image-to-pixel generation (I2P), where the model reconstructs a given image in pixel format, and pixel understanding , where the model identifies the underlying concept from a textual palette-and-grid representation generated by either an algorithmic or a model-based pixel oracle. Our evaluation shows that frontier LLMs already exhibit substantial pixel-generation capabilities, with leading models producing recognizable T2P outputs and competitive I2P reconstructions. Their behavior, however, depends strongly on target resolution. For many models, both visual quality and quantitative performance peak at an intermediate resolution, with 64 × 64 64\times 64 often performing worse than 32 × 32 32\times 32 , while GPT-6 Astra exhibits notably better robustness. We therefore conduct a fine-grained resolution-scaling study and find that, except for Astra’s consistently strong performance, most evaluated models initially improve but eventually decline as resolution increases. Viewing resolution as a measure of visual abstraction, these model-specific performance peaks suggest that different models are most effective at different levels of abstraction. Pixel understanding exhibits a similar ranking across models and correlates strongly with generation performance, suggesting that the connection between visual understanding and generation persists for pixel-based interface. The observed connection between pixel generation and visual understanding raises a natural question of whether reconstructing an input image can serve as a training objective to improve a model’s visual understanding. Reconstruction Alignment (RecA) ( Xie et al., 2026 ) shows that reconstruction-aligned visual representations can improve image generation, but whether reconstruction can also enhance visual understanding remains underexplored. Motivated by this, we propose Pixel Reconstruction Tuning (PRT), which augments post-training with trajectories that describe an image, explain an automatically constructed color palette, and reconstruct the image as a pixel grid. In a controlled experiment with Molmo2-4B, we start from its pretraining checkpoint and post-train it on 500k LLaVA-OneVision-1.5 instructions mixed with PRT examples. Incorporating PRT data improves average performance across 16 visual-centric benchmarks. Ablations varying the number of PRT examples from 1k to 8k show consistent improvements across all tested data scales. A complementary study with Qwen3-VL further shows that Pixel data can regularize post-training when incorporated into a general instruction mixture. Our contributions are summarized below: • A unified interface for evaluating pixel capabilities. We introduce PixelBench, a shared text-based pixel interface for evaluating frontier LLMs on both pixel generation and understanding. • Capability limits at increasing resolutions. We characterize model-specific performance peaks and failure modes. GPT-6 Astra remains robust as resolution increases, while other evaluated models generally improve and then decline. • Pixels as training supervision. We propose Pixel Reconstruction Tuning (PRT), which uses pixel reconstruction as a post-training objective. Starting from the Molmo2-4B pretraining checkpoint, incorporating PRT data into general instruction tuning consistently improves performance. sections.heading: 2.1 Pixels as a Visual Representation
sections.text: Pixel art is a compact visual output format. Its restricted palette and raster structure can preserve recognizable colors and shapes while limiting the number of symbols that a model must generate. Related representations are commonly used in icons, pictograms, low-resolution displays, and digital graphics. In this work, pixel art refers specifically to a palette-indexed raster with two components: a palette of RGB colors and an S × S S\times S grid of palette indices. Each grid entry selects the color of one pixel. The representation is human-interpretable and deterministic to render, and can be expressed using the model’s existing text vocabulary. We serialize the palette and index grid as JSON. The palette field contains two to eight opaque RGB colors in #RRGGBB format, and the pixels field contains the S S rows of palette indices. Rendering maps each index to its corresponding RGB value. Figure 2 shows rendered examples and their palettes.

sections.heading: 2.2 Benchmark Introduction and Design
sections.text: We introduce PixelBench to probe how much image-generation capability a language model can express through its native token interface. Unlike SVG and CAD, which describe images through high-level geometric primitives, our palette-indexed grids specify raster values directly: each generated grid entry corresponds to one rendered pixel, and rendering requires only a deterministic palette lookup. PixelBench therefore evaluates visual generation through a representation closer to the native form of raster images, without relying on a learned image tokenizer or decoder. Section 2.2 defines the generation and understanding tasks, models, baselines, and protocol; Section 2.3 specifies the metrics; and Section 2.4 presents the main results. We find that current models already exhibit substantial pixel-image generation ability through their text interface, while their pixel-understanding performance closely tracks their generation performance. Generation quality does not consistently improve with output resolution, as further analyzed in Section 3 . Tasks and datasets. In text-to-pixel generation (T2P), a model maps an English object label to a recognizable icon without a reference image. We use 100 concrete concepts spanning five categories (Appendix H ). In image-to-pixel generation (I2P), a vision encoder supplies a natural image and the model reconstructs it while preserving subject identity, pose, composition, and dominant colors. We sample one validation image from each of 100 ImageNet-1K classes ( Deng et al., 2009 ) and center-crop it to 256 × 256 256\times 256 (Appendix I ); the category is withheld. Every item in both generation tasks is evaluated at 16 2 16^{2} , 32 2 32^{2} , and 64 2 64^{2} , yielding 300 instances per task and model. In pixel understanding , a model receives only the textual serialization of an RGB palette and index grid and selects the concept from ten candidates. Inputs come from deterministic PIA-reduced reconstructions and GPT-6 Astra I2P generations (Astra-I2P), each with 100 questions at each resolution. Models and baselines. We evaluate Gemini 3.6 Flash ( Google DeepMind, 2026b ) , GPT-5.6 Sol ( OpenAI, 2026a ) , GPT-6 Astra ( OpenAI, 2026b ) , Claude Opus 5 ( Anthropic, 2026 ) , Seed-2.1 Pro ( ByteDance Seed, 2026 ) , and Kimi K3 ( Kimi Team, 2026 ) on both generation tasks and pixel understanding in a zero-shot setting. DeepSeek V4 Pro ( DeepSeek-AI, 2026 ) is included as a supplementary model for T2P and pixel understanding, but not for I2P generation. Detailed task-specific inference settings, including temperature, reasoning configuration, output-token limits, and samples per item, are reported in Appendix E . For I2P, we additionally compare against three representative palette-matched algorithms: nearest-neighbor sampling followed by median-cut quantization ( Heckbert, 1982 ) ; SSIM-optimal downscaling followed by median cut ( Öztireli & Gross, 2015 ) ; and a reduced Pixelated Image Abstraction pipeline ( Gerstner et al., 2012 ) that combines SLIC regions ( Achanta et al., 2012 ) with an eight-color weighted k k -means palette. The complete ten-method comparison and implementation details are in Appendix L . Generation protocol. Both generation tasks use the palette-indexed representation in Figure 2 : two to eight opaque RGB colors and an exactly sized index grid, with task-specific prompts. Successfully returned outputs with invalid JSON, palette references, or grid sizes receive zero; rate limits and token-limit truncations are retried, raising the limit when needed. Pixel understanding directly presents the serialized grid and ten choices, with no rendered image. Prompts are in Appendix G .

sections.heading: 2.3 Evaluation Metrics
sections.text: Text-to-Pixel metrics. Using the paired SigLIP-SO400M text and vision encoders ( Zhai et al., 2023 ) , we retrieve text candidates represented as “a pixel art icon depicting {label}.” The main table reports 500-way Top-1 and a complementary VLM-as-judge score from Gemini 3.5 Flash ( Google DeepMind, 2026a ) , whose 0-100 rubric prompt is in Appendix G.2 . The 100-way Top-1 and MRR diagnostics are in Appendix K ; retrieval definitions and vocabulary are in Appendices F and J . Image-to-Pixel metrics. We report 100-way Top-1 by embedding each generated output and the 100 candidate source images with the same SigLIP vision encoder. We additionally compute paired cosine similarity using pooled SigLIP features and DINOv2-Large CLS features ( Oquab et al., 2024 ) , which measure semantic and appearance-level similarity to the source, respectively. For both T2P and I2P, invalid outputs count as retrieval misses or zero similarity. We also report the Valid and Flat rates. Valid is the percentage of outputs with well-formed JSON, valid palette references, and the required grid size; Flat is the percentage of outputs that are valid but render to a single color. Pixel-understanding metric. We report 10-way recognition accuracy from the serialized palette-and-grid inputs. Each resolution contains 100 questions, so each source average covers 300 questions and the overall average covers all 600. Random-choice accuracy is 10%.

sections.heading: 3 Resolution Scaling and Failure Modes
sections.text: The main results suggest that higher resolution is not uniformly better: for many models in both T2P and I2P, 64 2 64^{2} underperforms 32 2 32^{2} (Tables 1 and 2 ). To examine this behavior more closely, we sweep GPT-6 Astra, GPT-5.6 Sol, Claude Opus 5, and Gemini 3.6 Flash over ten resolutions from 16 2 16^{2} to 128 2 128^{2} . The number of predicted grid positions grows quadratically with side length: relative to 16 2 16^{2} , 64 2 64^{2} and 128 2 128^{2} require 16 × \times and 64 × \times as many pixel indices. Resolution scaling therefore increases both representational capacity and the burden of coordinating a long spatial output. Text-to-Pixel Generation. The left two panels of Figure 4 report 500-way retrieval and VLM-as-judge quality, showing that increasing resolution does not consistently improve performance under either metric. GPT-6 Astra maintains strong performance across resolutions, with its judge score remaining near its peak through 96 2 96^{2} and declining only modestly at the two highest resolutions. GPT-5.6 Sol fluctuates after an early peak, while Claude Opus 5 exhibits oscillating retrieval performance but a clearer downward trend under VLM judging. Gemini 3.6 Flash shows the sharpest degradation at high resolutions, particularly beyond 64 2 64^{2} . The consistent agreement between retrieval and judge-based evaluations also suggests that the lack of monotonic improvement with resolution is not an artifact of the retrieval metric. Image-to-Pixel Generation. The right two panels reveal a clearer scaling pattern. GPT-6 Astra increasingly benefits from larger grids, with both retrieval accuracy and DINO similarity remaining strong at the highest resolutions. In contrast, the other models generally peak at intermediate resolutions and then decline. These results suggest that larger grids offer additional expressive capacity, but only GPT-6 Astra can translate this capacity into more faithful reconstructions. Figure 5 : Qualitative I2P resolution sweep. Two source images (left) are reconstructed from 16 2 16^{2} to 128 2 128^{2} ; rows show GPT-6 Astra, GPT-5.6 Sol, Claude Opus 5, and Gemini 3.6 Flash. Astra remains strongest and adds coherent detail as resolution grows; GPT-5.6 Sol collapses to a lower effective resolution, Claude mechanically repeats central details in one case and fails to recover fine architectural structure in the other, and Gemini increasingly omits the subject or other key structures. To inspect these differences directly, Figure 5 shows two I2P examples across the same resolution sweep. GPT-6 Astra progressively adds texture, sharper boundaries, and architectural detail while preserving the subject and overall layout. GPT-5.6 Sol instead exhibits an effective-resolution collapse : despite the increasing nominal grid size, its outputs become dominated by large color blocks. This behavior can preserve a coarse semantic layout, but it underuses the available grid and reduces fidelity. Claude Opus 5 shows different failures across the two inputs. In the upper example, it mechanically repeats details from the central region, sacrificing the fidelity of the global reconstruction. In the lower indoor-architecture example, it preserves only a coarse layout and fails to recover fine structural details. Gemini 3.6 Flash degrades most severely, with the subject or key structures gradually vanishing at high resolutions. Together, these examples expose three high-resolution failure modes: effective-resolution collapse, repetitive local patterns that disrupt global structure, and omission of the subject or other key structures. They also reveal a broader consistency gap across resolutions. Beyond how effectively models use additional grid positions, other models can produce substantially different reconstructions as resolution increases, whereas Astra preserves subject identity, composition, and overall appearance across scales. Astra’s advantage is therefore not merely its ability to produce longer outputs, but its ability to organize additional grid positions into coherent details while maintaining a stable reconstruction. Representative T2P cases in Appendix B exhibit the same failure modes.

sections.heading: 4 Pixel Reconstruction Tuning
sections.text: The strong correlation between pixel generation and pixel understanding in PixelBench raises a training question: can pixel generation itself serve as an objective that improves a VLM’s general visual understanding? RecA ( Xie et al., 2026 ) explores a related idea for unified multimodal models, training them to reconstruct input images from their visual representations and thereby improving general image generation and editing. For visual understanding, however, conventional image-text and VQA supervision provides sparse, non-unique textual targets rather than dense supervision over visual content. Pixel generation provides such a target by requiring a VLM to reconstruct its input as a palette-indexed pixel grid, turning the image itself into deterministic, spatially aligned training supervision. We term this approach Pixel Reconstruction Tuning (PRT).

sections.heading: 4.1 Data and Training
sections.text: Pixel Reconstruction Tuning Data Construction. We sample images from a 20k-image PixMo-Cap pool ( Deitke et al., 2025 ) after removing exact matches with evaluation images. To avoid distortion from square reconstruction targets, we discard images with aspect ratios above 1.33. We also exclude text-heavy and multi-panel images that cannot be faithfully represented at resolutions of 16 2 16^{2} to 32 2 32^{2} . We render both resolutions with the PIA-reduced procedure (Appendix L ) and compute the SigLIP2 cosine similarity between each rendered pixel image and its source image. We retain the top 40% at 16 2 16^{2} and the top 80% at 32 2 32^{2} . For each retained image, we query Gemini 3.8 Flash to write an image description and summarize the colors in the algorithmically constructed palette. We package these with the grid using <CAPTION> , <PALETTE> , and <GRID> , while keeping the palette and grid values deterministic. The retained examples are our PRT data (see Appendix D ). sections.heading: 4.2 Main Results
sections.text: PRT Improves VLM Performance. sections.heading: 5 Concluding Remarks
sections.text: We introduce PixelBench, a text-based interface for direct pixel generation and understanding without a learned image tokenizer or decoder. Across T2P, I2P, and understanding tasks, frontier models exhibit substantial yet uneven capabilities, with model-specific resolution peaks. GPT-6 Astra remains robust as grid resolution increases, whereas most other models initially improve before declining. Beyond evaluation, we introduce PRT, which transforms deterministic palettes and grids into instruction trajectories. By combining general instruction data with curated PRT data, we post-train Molmo2-4B from its pretraining checkpoint, improving performance across 16 visual-centric benchmarks. The performance gain can also be observed in Qwen3-VL across different scales. These findings highlight the dual role of explicit pixels as a behavioral probe for evaluating visual capabilities and a practical training signal for improving them.

sections.heading: A.1 Symbolic Visual Representations
sections.text: A growing line of work represents visual content as a discrete symbol sequence that a renderer executes, rather than as a dense array of pixels. On the understanding side, SGP-Bench evaluates whether language models can infer the semantics of SVG and CAD programs without seeing their renderings and improves this ability through Symbolic Instruction Tuning ( Qiu et al., 2025 ) , while VGBench and SVGenius broaden evaluation to editing and generation across many formats, domains, and complexity levels ( Zou et al., 2024 ; Chen et al., 2025 ) . On the generation side, models emit SVG code or executable CAD programs directly ( Chen et al., 2026b ; Rodriguez et al., 2025 ; Xing et al., 2025 ; Wu et al., 2025 ; Khan et al., 2024 ; Rukhovich et al., 2025 ; Zhuang et al., 2026 ) , and Sharma et al. (2024) use rendering code as a stand-in for pixels, demonstrating that text-only models encode substantial visual knowledge. Together, these studies show that general-purpose models encode usable geometric knowledge in symbolic form, although their performance degrades when precise spatial and structural fidelity is required. Two properties separate that setting from ours. A program mediates between model and image, so the renderer supplies geometry and resolution independence and each primitive covers many pixels; token-based generative models instead keep the raster form but substitute a learned codebook whose vocabulary is opaque and whose decoding requires the paired detokenizer ( Chen et al., 2020 ; Chameleon Team, 2024 ; Wang et al., 2026 ) . PixelBench asks for an explicit palette and per-pixel indices, so rendering is a table lookup and every emitted symbol is one spatial location. The closest prior evaluation of this format is Pixel Art Bench, a web leaderboard that ranks 24 × 24 24\times 24 grids for seven subjects by LLM-judged Elo ( Emergent Mind, 2026 ) . Color-index grids also appear in abstract reasoning ( Chollet, 2019 ) . PixelBench broadens this to text-to-pixel and image-to-pixel generation over 100 concepts and 100 natural images at three resolutions, adds a complementary pixel-understanding evaluation, replaces judge-based ranking with deterministic retrieval and fidelity metrics, and compares against palette-matched pixelization and downscaling algorithms ( Öztireli & Gross, 2015 ; Weber et al., 2016 ; Wu et al., 2022 ) .

sections.heading: A.2 Vision-Language Training and Visual Representations
sections.text: Contemporary VLMs pair a pretrained visual encoder with a language model through a connector, aligned by image-text pretraining and visual instruction tuning ( Radford et al., 2021 ; Zhai et al., 2023 ; Alayrac et al., 2022 ; Li et al., 2023 ; Liu et al., 2023 ; Dai et al., 2023 ; Liu et al., 2024a ) . Controlled ablations attribute much of the reported progress to the unimodal backbones and to training data rather than to the connector ( Karamcheti et al., 2024 ; Laurençon et al., 2024 ) , and a parallel body of work stresses the composition, quality, and cleanliness of that data: vision-centric mixtures sharpen fine-grained perception ( Tong et al., 2024a ) , curated non-distilled and decontaminated corpora improve generalization ( Deitke et al., 2025 ; Wiedmann et al., 2025 ) , and benchmark audits show that apparent gains can stem from leakage or from questions answerable without the image ( Chen et al., 2024 ) . Across these pipelines the supervision target is language, whatever the visual input. That choice has consequences: distinctions lost by the encoder propagate into the assembled model ( Tong et al., 2024b ) , which remains unreliable on low-level spatial queries ( Rahmanzadehgervi et al., 2024 ; Fu et al., 2024 ) . Objectives that require reproducing visual detail instead yield transferable representations ( He et al., 2022 ; Chen et al., 2020 ) , and MetaMorph finds understanding and visual generation mutually beneficial ( Tong et al., 2025 ) . Reconstruction Alignment (RecA) conditions unified multimodal models on their own visual encoder representations and trains them to reconstruct the input image, thereby connecting visual understanding and generation ( Xie et al., 2026 ) . PRT studies an analogous objective for VLMs without a dedicated image generator: predicting the palette-index grid itself through the existing vocabulary, with no learned image tokenizer or decoder. Our primary protocol starts from a Molmo2 pretraining checkpoint and adds caption-palette-grid trajectories to a fixed 500k-example instruction mixture. Appendix D additionally reports the earlier Qwen3-VL experiments, where pixel targets are added to FineVision post-training as a regularizer.

sections.heading: Appendix B Additional Resolution-Scaling Examples
sections.text: Figure 6 : Model-dependent resolution behavior in T2P. Each case group shows GPT-5.6 Sol, Gemini 3.6 Flash, and Claude Opus 5 at 16 2 16^{2} , 32 2 32^{2} , and 64 2 64^{2} . Higher nominal resolution can yield finer detail, coarse effective pixels, or degraded global structure depending on the model and prompt. These cases instantiate the same three failure modes observed in the qualitative I2P sweep. GPT-5.6 Sol exhibits effective-resolution underutilization : its 64 2 64^{2} skateboard and fire are dominated by blocks roughly one-eighth of the canvas width, giving them a granularity closer to an 8 × 8 8\times 8 grid. The outputs remain recognizable, but the additional positions contribute little detail. Gemini 3.6 Flash uses finer boundaries and local variation, but these local patterns can disrupt global structure: at 64 2 64^{2} , its skateboard collapses to a diagonal stroke, its star loses the five-point structure, and its fire loses a coherent silhouette. The latter cases also omit identity-bearing structures. Claude Opus 5 varies by prompt: it preserves the depicted objects in these examples while using the higher-resolution grid, but its aggregate T2P performance fluctuates across resolutions and does not sustain its intermediate-resolution peak.

sections.heading: D.1 Molmo2 Pixel-Trajectory Construction
sections.text: Image pool and filtering. Pixel trajectories use PixMo-Cap images with human-written dense captions. We first construct a 20k-image pool and expand it with previously unused images for the 4k and 8k sets. Exact hash matches to evaluation images are removed. We reject examples whose captions indicate screenshots, webpages, user interfaces, documents, posters, text, charts, diagrams, infographics, collages, or multi-panel layouts because text-heavy and composite content cannot be faithfully represented at 16 2 16^{2} - 32 2 32^{2} . Because PIA-reduced converts every source to a square grid, we also reject images with aspect ratio above 1.33 to avoid substantial geometric distortion. Recognizability and grid construction. For each candidate, we construct 16 2 16^{2} and 32 2 32^{2} eight-color grids using the PIA-reduced procedure (Appendix L ). We nearest-neighbor upscale each grid and compute its paired cosine similarity with the source image using SigLIP2-base-patch16-224. At each resolution, candidates are ranked by this similarity; we retain the top 40% at 16 2 16^{2} and the top 80% at 32 2 32^{2} . Images are unique within every set. The 2k set is balanced across 16 2 16^{2} and 32 2 32^{2} ; 4k and 8k are nested extensions whose new rows use previously unused images. Natural-language trajectory. Gemini 3.8 Flash receives the original image, upscaled ground-truth grid, one mask visualization per palette letter, the PixMo caption, and measured palette/layout hints. At temperature 0.4 and thinking budget 2,048, it writes only the caption and palette explanation; the palette and grid remain deterministic. The response must discuss every palette letter exactly once and in order, otherwise it is retried up to three times. Three paraphrased user prompts are assigned deterministically. Median target lengths are 1,693 characters at 16 2 16^{2} and 2,739 at 32 2 32^{2} .

sections.heading: D.5 Fixed Data Amount and Training Steps
sections.text: To compare reconstruction tuning under matched training conditions, we fix both the amount of training data and the number of updates. FV-only contains 64,000 FineVision occurrences. Each Pixel configuration replaces 3,000 of those occurrences with pixel-reconstruction examples, so every fine-tuning run uses exactly 64,000 occurrences and stops at 1,000 optimizer steps. The single-resolution variants use eight-color PIA-reduced targets at 16 2 16^{2} , 32 2 32^{2} , or 64 2 64^{2} in separate runs, reusing the same 3,000 unique source-image IDs across runs. The mixed variant assigns each image from that batch to exactly one resolution, approximately evenly, using sampling seed 0. Source-image sampling is without replacement, so no image is repeated within a run. All fine-tuning runs use training seed 42, four GPUs with DeepSpeed ZeRO-2, per-GPU batch size 4, and four gradient accumulation steps; the 4B runs use NVIDIA A100 80GB GPUs. These settings match the number of training occurrences and optimizer steps; target sequence length still grows with grid size. Training-seed sensitivity. sections.heading: D.6 Limitations
sections.text: The main Molmo comparison adds Pixel trajectories to OV rather than replacing OV rows, so the 2k condition receives eight additional updates. We also do not compare against alternative auxiliary objectives on the same images, such as caption-only trajectories. We therefore cannot fully separate the palette-index grid from additional image exposure or its accompanying language supervision. Pixel trajectories are longer than typical responses, so their token share exceeds their 0.4% share of examples. The 2k Benchmark-average effect is small ( + 0.5 +0.5 points), has a standardized difference of z = 1.5 z=1.5 , and is positive in three of four matched seed pairs. The 1k, 4k, and 8k settings have only two seeds each, and the observed gains do not increase with quantity. These results support a small, consistent aggregate benefit, not a data-scaling claim. The secondary Qwen controls compare PRT against FineVision-only tuning and do not isolate pixel targets from additional image exposure. Their additive runs also contain 47 extra updates. The fixed-data, equal-step experiment above addresses update count but replaces some FineVision supervision, leaving the auxiliary-objective comparison unresolved.

sections.text: Judge inference and stability. We use Gemini 3.5 Flash with temperature 0, thinking budget 0, a maximum of 1,536 output tokens, and one sample per item. sections.heading: Appendix L Algorithmic Image-to-Pixel Baselines in Full
sections.text: Each method either combines a spatial downscaling stage with a subsequent color quantization stage or jointly determines the output regions and palette. We set the palette size to eight for all constrained methods and evaluate them on the same 100 ImageNet validation crops used for the VLMs. Tier 0: simple resampling. Nearest-neighbor sampling selects the source-cell center, while box filtering averages the corresponding source patch. Both are followed by median-cut quantization ( Heckbert, 1982 ) . Tier 1: linear filters. Bicubic and Lanczos interpolation use standard fixed resampling kernels before median-cut quantization. These methods allocate the output resolution uniformly across the image. Tier 2: content-adaptive downscaling. DPID ( Weber et al., 2016 ) weights input pixels according to their deviation from a local guidance color; we evaluate λ ∈ { 0.5 , 1.0 } \lambda\in\{0.5,1.0\} . SSIM-optimal downscaling ( Öztireli & Gross, 2015 ) minimizes structural dissimilarity using local image statistics. Both methods are followed by median-cut quantization. Tier 3: pixel-art-specific methods. Pyxelate 1 1 1 https://github.com/sedthh/pyxelate uses Sobel-gradient information to merge local cells and estimates an eight-color palette with a Bayesian Gaussian mixture. We use version 2.1 or later with sobel=3 , depth=1 , and dithering disabled. Pixelated Image Abstraction (PIA) ( Gerstner et al., 2012 ) jointly constructs output regions and a reduced palette. The reference implementation uses modified SLIC mapping, mass-constrained deterministic annealing ( Rose, 1998 ) , bilateral superpixel smoothing, and a saturation factor of 1.1 1.1 . PIA (reduced) retains SLIC with compactness m = 45 m=45 , replaces annealing with weighted eight-means over superpixel colors, and omits bilateral smoothing and saturation adjustment.

Haoquan Zhang Feiyang Liu Juanxi Tian Wanhua Li Haodong Duan Weiyang Liu Affiliation: CUHK SCUT NTU Singapore † Corresponding author Project Page Abstract Large language models (LLMs) can generate visual assets through text-based formats such as SVG and CAD, but these symbolic representations describe images using high-level primitives rather than explicit raster values. We ask whether LLMs can instead generate pixel images directly through their existing vocabulary, without a learned image tokenizer or decoder. We introduce PixelBench, a benchmark for text-to-pixel (T2P) and image-to-pixel (I2P) generation across multiple resolutions, together with a complementary pixel-understanding evaluation. Models generate an RGB color palette followed by a grid of indices specifying the palette color of each output pixel. In T2P, the strongest models produce recognizable images directly from text. In I2P, the strongest models outperform palette-matched downsampling and specialized pixelization algorithms at low resolutions. Pixel-understanding performance correlates strongly with generation performance. A resolution-scaling study shows that pixel-generation performance often improves initially before declining at high resolutions. Finally, we introduce Pixel Reconstruction Tuning (PRT), which augments visual instruction tuning with caption-palette-grid trajectories. We post-train Molmo2-4B from its pretraining checkpoint by mixing general instruction data with our curated PRT data, improving performance across 16 visual-centric benchmarks, indicating that explicit pixel reconstruction can provide useful auxiliary supervision. Figure 1 : Zero-shot text-to-pixel generation by large language models. Left: pixel images generated at different resolutions. Right: our generation protocol, in which the model defines a color palette and outputs a numerical grid whose entries index the palette colors. See Figure 3 for image-to-pixel generation. 1 Introduction Large language models (LLMs) were originally developed to predict the next token in natural-language sequences. The same autoregressive training paradigm has since produced strong code-generation capabilities. Some generated code, including SVG code and CAD programs, can be rendered into images, providing an interface for probing how LLMs express visual information ( Sharma et al., 2024 ; Qiu et al., 2025 ; Chen et al., 2026b ; Rodriguez et al., 2025 ; Xing et al., 2025 ; Khan et al., 2024 ) . However, these formats describe images using semantically meaningful, high-level primitives and are therefore one step away from actual visual appearance: a renderer expands each primitive into many pixels. By contrast, RGB rasters provide a more direct and ubiquitous representation of digital images, with each spatial location in a two-dimensional grid storing a color value. Most modern image generators map learned visual tokens or latent representations to pixels through dedicated decoders ( Chameleon Team, 2024 ; Wang et al., 2026 ) . Prior work has also trained specialized autoregressive image models to generate images directly in raster space ( van den Oord et al., 2016a ; van den Oord et al., 2016b ; Parmar et al., 2018 ; Chen et al., 2020 ) . These studies demonstrate the feasibility of direct pixel generation, but rely on models specifically designed and trained for image modeling. To better investigate pixel-based visual understanding and generation, we ask the following question: Can LLMs directly generate and understand visual content pixel by pixel? To address this research question, we introduce PixelBench , a benchmark for evaluating LLMs on direct pixel generation and understanding. PixelBench uses a palette-indexed raster representation: the model first defines a palette of up to eight RGB colors and then generates a grid of palette indices, with each grid position specifying the color of one pixel. This interface needs no learned tokenizer, image decoder, or architectural change. PixelBench evaluates three tasks: text-to-pixel generation (T2P), where a model generates a recognizable pixel image from an object label, image-to-pixel generation (I2P), where the model reconstructs a given image in pixel format, and pixel understanding , where the model identifies the underlying concept from a textual palette-and-grid representation generated by either an algorithmic or a model-based pixel oracle. Our evaluation shows that frontier LLMs already exhibit substantial pixel-generation capabilities, with leading models producing recognizable T2P outputs and competitive I2P reconstructions. Their behavior, however, depends strongly on target resolution. For many models, both visual quality and quantitative performance peak at an intermediate resolution, with 64 × 64 64\times 64 often performing worse than 32 × 32 32\times 32 , while GPT-6 Astra exhibits notably better robustness. We therefore conduct a fine-grained resolution-scaling study and find that, except for Astra’s consistently strong performance, most evaluated models initially improve but eventually decline as resolution increases. Viewing resolution as a measure of visual abstraction, these model-specific performance peaks suggest that different models are most effective at different levels of abstraction. Pixel understanding exhibits a similar ranking across models and correlates strongly with generation performance, suggesting that the connection between visual understanding and generation persists for pixel-based interface. The observed connection between pixel generation and visual understanding raises a natural question of whether reconstructing an input image can serve as a training objective to improve a model’s visual understanding. Reconstruction Alignment (RecA) ( Xie et al., 2026 ) shows that reconstruction-aligned visual representations can improve image generation, but whether reconstruction can also enhance visual understanding remains underexplored. Motivated by this, we propose Pixel Reconstruction Tuning (PRT), which augments post-training with trajectories that describe an image, explain an automatically constructed color palette, and reconstruct the image as a pixel grid. In a controlled experiment with Molmo2-4B, we start from its pretraining checkpoint and post-train it on 500k LLaVA-OneVision-1.5 instructions mixed with PRT examples. Incorporating PRT data improves average performance across 16 visual-centric benchmarks. Ablations varying the number of PRT examples from 1k to 8k show consistent improvements across all tested data scales. A complementary study with Qwen3-VL further shows that Pixel data can regularize post-training when incorporated into a general instruction mixture. Our contributions are summarized below: • A unified interface for evaluating pixel capabilities. We introduce PixelBench, a shared text-based pixel interface for evaluating frontier LLMs on both pixel generation and understanding. • Capability limits at increasing resolutions. We characterize model-specific performance peaks and failure modes. GPT-6 Astra remains robust as resolution increases, while other evaluated models generally improve and then decline. • Pixels as training supervision. We propose Pixel Reconstruction Tuning (PRT), which uses pixel reconstruction as a post-training objective. Starting from the Molmo2-4B pretraining checkpoint, incorporating PRT data into general instruction tuning consistently improves performance. Figure 2 : Examples of palette-indexed pixel representations. Each example pairs a compact color palette (top) with a 16 × 16 16\times 16 grid of palette indices (bottom). The mushroom, bee, frog, and rocket remain recognizable despite the low resolution and restricted palettes. 2 PixelBench : Evaluating Pixel Understanding and Generation 2.1 Pixels as a Visual Representation Pixel art is a compact visual output format. Its restricted palette and raster structure can preserve recognizable colors and shapes while limiting the number of symbols that a model must generate. Related representations are commonly used in icons, pictograms, low-resolution displays, and digital graphics. In this work, pixel art refers specifically to a palette-indexed raster with two components: a palette of RGB colors and an S × S S\times S grid of palette indices. Each grid entry selects the color of one pixel. The representation is human-interpretable and deterministic to render, and can be expressed using the model’s existing text vocabulary. We serialize the palette and index grid as JSON. The palette field contains two to eight opaque RGB colors in #RRGGBB format, and the pixels field contains the S S rows of palette indices. Rendering maps each index to its corresponding RGB value. Figure 2 shows rendered examples and their palettes. 2.2 Benchmark Introduction and Design We introduce PixelBench to probe how much image-generation capability a language model can express through its native token interface. Unlike SVG and CAD, which describe images through high-level geometric primitives, our palette-indexed grids specify raster values directly: each generated grid entry corresponds to one rendered pixel, and rendering requires only a deterministic palette lookup. PixelBench therefore evaluates visual generation through a representation closer to the native form of raster images, without relying on a learned image tokenizer or decoder. Section 2.2 defines the generation and understanding tasks, models, baselines, and protocol; Section 2.3 specifies the metrics; and Section 2.4 presents the main results. We find that current models already exhibit substantial pixel-image generation ability through their text interface, while their pixel-understanding performance closely tracks their generation performance. Generation quality does not consistently improve with output resolution, as further analyzed in Section 3 . Tasks and datasets. In text-to-pixel generation (T2P), a model maps an English object label to a recognizable icon without a reference image. We use 100 concrete concepts spanning five categories (Appendix H ). In image-to-pixel generation (I2P), a vision encoder supplies a natural image and the model reconstructs it while preserving subject identity, pose, composition, and dominant colors. We sample one validation image from each of 100 ImageNet-1K classes ( Deng et al., 2009 ) and center-crop it to 256 × 256 256\times 256 (Appendix I ); the category is withheld. Every item in both generation tasks is evaluated at 16 2 16^{2} , 32 2 32^{2} , and 64 2 64^{2} , yielding 300 instances per task and model. In pixel understanding , a model receives only the textual serialization of an RGB palette and index grid and selects the concept from ten candidates. Inputs come from deterministic PIA-reduced reconstructions and GPT-6 Astra I2P generations (Astra-I2P), each with 100 questions at each resolution. Models and baselines. We evaluate Gemini 3.6 Flash ( Google DeepMind, 2026b ) , GPT-5.6 Sol ( OpenAI, 2026a ) , GPT-6 Astra ( OpenAI, 2026b ) , Claude Opus 5 ( Anthropic, 2026 ) , Seed-2.1 Pro ( ByteDance Seed, 2026 ) , and Kimi K3 ( Kimi Team, 2026 ) on both generation tasks and pixel understanding in a zero-shot setting. DeepSeek V4 Pro ( DeepSeek-AI, 2026 ) is included as a supplementary model for T2P and pixel understanding, but not for I2P generation. Detailed task-specific inference settings, including temperature, reasoning configuration, output-token limits, and samples per item, are reported in Appendix E . For I2P, we additionally compare against three representative palette-matched algorithms: nearest-neighbor sampling followed by median-cut quantization ( Heckbert, 1982 ) ; SSIM-optimal downscaling followed by median cut ( Öztireli & Gross, 2015 ) ; and a reduced Pixelated Image Abstraction pipeline ( Gerstner et al., 2012 ) that combines SLIC regions ( Achanta et al., 2012 ) with an eight-color weighted k k -means palette. The complete ten-method comparison and implementation details are in Appendix L . Generation protocol. Both generation tasks use the palette-indexed representation in Figure 2 : two to eight opaque RGB colors and an exactly sized index grid, with task-specific prompts. Successfully returned outputs with invalid JSON, palette references, or grid sizes receive zero; rate limits and token-limit truncations are retried, raising the limit when needed. Pixel understanding directly presents the serialized grid and ten choices, with no rendered image. Prompts are in Appendix G . 2.3 Evaluation Metrics Text-to-Pixel metrics. Using the paired SigLIP-SO400M text and vision encoders ( Zhai et al., 2023 ) , we retrieve text candidates represented as “a pixel art icon depicting {label}.” The main table reports 500-way Top-1 and a complementary VLM-as-judge score from Gemini 3.5 Flash ( Google DeepMind, 2026a ) , whose 0-100 rubric prompt is in Appendix G.2 . The 100-way Top-1 and MRR diagnostics are in Appendix K ; retrieval definitions and vocabulary are in Appendices F and J . Image-to-Pixel metrics. We report 100-way Top-1 by embedding each generated output and the 100 candidate source images with the same SigLIP vision encoder. Beyond how effectively models use additional grid positions, other models can produce substantially different reconstructions as resolution increases, whereas Astra preserves subject identity, composition, and overall appearance across scales. Astra’s advantage is therefore not merely its ability to produce longer outputs, but its ability to organize additional grid positions into coherent details while maintaining a stable reconstruction. Representative T2P cases in Appendix B exhibit the same failure modes. 4 Pixel Reconstruction Tuning The strong correlation between pixel generation and pixel understanding in PixelBench raises a training question: can pixel generation itself serve as an objective that improves a VLM’s general visual understanding? RecA ( Xie et al., 2026 ) explores a related idea for unified multimodal models, training them to reconstruct input images from their visual representations and thereby improving general image generation and editing. For visual understanding, however, conventional image-text and VQA supervision provides sparse, non-unique textual targets rather than dense supervision over visual content. Pixel generation provides such a target by requiring a VLM to reconstruct its input as a palette-indexed pixel grid, turning the image itself into deterministic, spatially aligned training supervision. We term this approach Pixel Reconstruction Tuning (PRT). 4.1 Data and Training Pixel Reconstruction Tuning Data Construction. We sample images from a 20k-image PixMo-Cap pool ( Deitke et al., 2025 ) after removing exact matches with evaluation images. To avoid distortion from square reconstruction targets, we discard images with aspect ratios above 1.33. We also exclude text-heavy and multi-panel images that cannot be faithfully represented at resolutions of 16 2 16^{2} to 32 2 32^{2} . We render both resolutions with the PIA-reduced procedure (Appendix L ) and compute the SigLIP2 cosine similarity between each rendered pixel image and its source image. We retain the top 40% at 16 2 16^{2} and the top 80% at 32 2 32^{2} . For each retained image, we query Gemini 3.8 Flash to write an image description and summarize the colors in the algorithmically constructed palette. We package these with the grid using <CAPTION> , <PALETTE> , and <GRID> , while keeping the palette and grid values deterministic. The retained examples are our PRT data (see Appendix D ). Across T2P, I2P, and understanding tasks, frontier models exhibit substantial yet uneven capabilities, with model-specific resolution peaks. GPT-6 Astra remains robust as grid resolution increases, whereas most other models initially improve before declining. Beyond evaluation, we introduce PRT, which transforms deterministic palettes and grids into instruction trajectories. By combining general instruction data with curated PRT data, we post-train Molmo2-4B from its pretraining checkpoint, improving performance across 16 visual-centric benchmarks. The performance gain can also be observed in Qwen3-VL across different scales. These findings highlight the dual role of explicit pixels as a behavioral probe for evaluating visual capabilities and a practical training signal for improving them.
